title: Lift up your gates (Psalm 23 [24])
hookLine: the earth is the Lord's, and the king of glory comes in

cards: A crowd climbs a hill toward a walled city, singing. At the front, carried on poles, is the ark, the gold-covered chest that, in Israel's scriptures, marks the presence of the invisible God. The city gates are shut.

The crowd calls up to them, the watchmen on the walls call back a question, and the crowd answers. Call and response, like a stadium chant. Psalm 23 in the Douay, 24 in most Bibles, may well be the script for that moment.

teach.b: It opens wide: "The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof: the world, and all they that dwell therein." The ground, the sea, every person on it.
Saint Paul quotes this line to settle an argument about food: eat what's sold in the market, he says, because the earth is the Lord's.
Then the question at the foot of the hill: "Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord: or who shall stand in his holy place?"
The answer isn't a bloodline or a title: "The innocent in hands, and clean of heart." Clean hands, meaning what you do. A clean heart, meaning what you want.
Then the gates: "Lift up your gates, O ye princes, and be ye lifted up, O eternal gates: and the King of Glory shall enter in."

teach.h: WHO IS THIS KING OF GLORY?
teach.b: From the wall, the challenge: "Who is this King of Glory?" And the crowd: the Lord who is strong and mighty. It happens twice, a chant that builds.
Christian readers have heard Christ here: some heard his entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, some the Ascension, heaven's gates opening.
An old Christian story tells of Christ going down to the dead on Holy Saturday, and the gates of the underworld hearing this very psalm before they break.

teach.h: THE DOOR KNOCKED WITH A CROSS.
teach.b: And in the older Roman rite of Palm Sunday, the procession stopped outside the shut church door, someone knocked with the foot of the cross, and the gates were sung open.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 23 [24] in the Liturgy of the Hours, sometimes as the opening Invitatory psalm, and hear it at Mass in Advent and on feasts like the Presentation of the Lord.

games.q: you're a watchman on the city wall. a singing crowd outside cries lift up your gates! what do you call back?
o: who is this King of Glory?
games.why: who is this King of Glory? and the crowd answers: the Lord who is strong and mighty. the exchange happens twice, building like a chant.

practice: Open a window or a door slowly, on purpose, and stand there breathing the outside air; if you can't reach one, picture a door in your home opening wide.

Think of the psalm's first line: the street, the neighbors, the weather, all of it the Lord's. If you pray, say lift up your gates, and let God in; if you don't, let the open door be a way of welcoming the day.

wordCard.voice: Attollite portas. Latin for lift up your gates, the psalm's cry at the city wall, so the King of Glory can come in. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: lift up your gates, the psalm's cry in the Vulgate, sung in chant and processions for centuries.

carryVoice: Your line: the earth is the lord's. Every bit of it, even the ordinary streets. Until tomorrow.
